title: Ext4 Filesystem Errors and Recovery
exclusions: Detects only collected kernel records that parse as the Linux ext4 `EXT4-fs error (device ...): function:line: ...` or `EXT4-fs error (device ...) in function:line: ...` forms. It does not alert on `EXT4-fs warning`, generic block-layer or JBD2 errors, user-space `Input/output error` text, an ext4 superblock error not emitted to the collected log, journal recovery without an ext4 error in the same five-minute bucket, or any record lost before forwarding. Forced read-only transitions are owned by UC-1.1.19. A `recovery complete` message means kernel journal replay completed; it does not prove that `e2fsck` ran, that every inconsistency was repaired, or that the device is healthy. This UC does not identify root cause, map a device to a mount point, perform repair, prove continuous coverage, or provide regulatory attestation. The base SPL applies no exception lookup.
evidence: After deployment, retain the versioned `linux_ext4_errors_5m` saved-search definition and schedule, dispatch and alert history, matching raw kernel records, parsed result fields, effective file-monitor configuration, source-coverage reconciliation, and dated positive/negative control-test output. For an incident, link the host/device mapping, surrounding kernel and storage records, change ticket, and storage-owner recovery disposition; retain any authorized offline `e2fsck` output separately. These artifacts show what the configured collector and search observed at recorded times; they do not prove uninterrupted collection, a clean filesystem, successful repair, or runtime validation by this documentation review.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index with `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog`, ingest `Jul 28 09:00:00 ext4-test kernel: EXT4-fs error (device dm-0): ext4_find_entry:1458: inode #2: comm test: reading directory lblock 0` and `Jul 28 09:01:00 ext4-test kernel: EXT4-fs (dm-0): recovery complete`, both with `host=ext4-test` in one five-minute bucket. Run the SPL with fixed bounds covering that bucket. Expect exactly one row with `device=dm-0`, `error_events=1`, `recovery_complete_events=1`, `kernel_functions=ext4_find_entry`, and `source_lines=1458`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In a separate five-minute bucket, ingest `EXT4-fs warning (device dm-0): ext4_dx_add_entry:2463: Directory index full!`, `EXT4-fs (dm-0): recovery complete`, `EXT4-fs (dm-0): Remounting filesystem read-only`, and `app[42]: EXT4-fs error reported by user`. The final search must return zero rows: warning, recovery-only, the separately owned read-only transition, and a look-alike without the kernel error signature do not satisfy the one-parsed-error threshold.

dataSources: Linux kernel messages persisted by the host logging stack to the one active text log that contains kernel records, commonly `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/kern.log`, or `/var/log/syslog`, collected by a Splunk Universal Forwarder native file monitor as the pretrained `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog` into the locally selected `index=os`. Required indexed fields are `_time`, `_raw`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`; the SPL derives `device`, `event_type`, `kernel_function`, `source_line`, `error_detail`, and five-minute error/recovery counts. `journalctl -k` and `dmesg` are host-side validation tools, not source types or polling inputs in this implementation.
app: Splunk Universal Forwarder native file-monitor input with Splunk's pretrained `linux_messages_syslog` sourcetype. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) is optional deployment context for broader host telemetry; this rule does not require or claim a dedicated ext4 scripted input.

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux

spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog "EXT4-fs" ("EXT4-fs error (device" OR "recovery complete" OR "INFO: recovery required on readonly filesystem")
| rex field=_raw "EXT4-fs error \(device\s+(?<error_device>[^)]+)\)(?::|\s+in)\s+(?<kernel_function>[^:\s]+):(?<source_line>\d+):\s+(?<error_detail>[^\r\n]+)"
| rex field=_raw "EXT4-fs \((?<recovery_device>[^)]+)\):\s+(?<recovery_message>INFO:\s+recovery required on readonly filesystem|recovery complete)"
| eval device=trim(coalesce(error_device,recovery_device)), source_line=tonumber(source_line), event_type=case(isnotnull(error_device),"filesystem_error",match(recovery_message,"^INFO:"),"recovery_required",recovery_message="recovery complete","recovery_complete")
| where isnotnull(device) AND isnotnull(event_type)
| eval event_time=_time, error_event=if(event_type="filesystem_error",1,0), recovery_required_event=if(event_type="recovery_required",1,0), recovery_complete_event=if(event_type="recovery_complete",1,0), error_time=if(event_type="filesystem_error",event_time,null()), error_sample=if(event_type="filesystem_error",_raw,null())
| bin _time span=5m
| stats sum(error_event) as error_events sum(recovery_required_event) as recovery_required_events sum(recovery_complete_event) as recovery_complete_events min(error_time) as first_error max(error_time) as last_error values(kernel_function) as kernel_functions values(source_line) as source_lines latest(error_detail) as sample_error_detail latest(error_sample) as sample_error values(source) as sources by _time host device
| where error_events>0
| sort 0 -_time host device
description: Returns one row per five-minute bucket, Linux host, and extracted ext4 device when at least one collected record matches a kernel-defined `EXT4-fs error (device ...)` form and yields a function and source line. The row counts matching error records and reports any exact ext4 journal-recovery-required or recovery-complete messages observed for that same host, device, and bucket; recovery context never cancels an error.
value: An ext4 metadata error can precede write failures, journal abort, protective read-only behavior, data unavailability, or an offline repair requirement while host and process health checks still pass. Prompt device- and function-level evidence helps Linux and storage owners contain risky writes, preserve incident context, assess application impact, and choose a controlled recovery path instead of attempting an unsafe live repair.
implementation: Monitor exactly one distribution-specific text log that persists kernel records, assign Splunk's pretrained `linux_messages_syslog` source type, and route it to the locally selected OS index. Verify the two kernel-defined ext4 error forms and recovery messages against raw events, then schedule `linux_ext4_errors_5m` every five minutes over a delayed completed bucket and trigger when the search returns any row. One parsed ext4 error record in five minutes is the initial threshold; recovery messages are context only.
visualization: Use a latest-first critical table with bucket, host, device, error count, first/last error, kernel functions, source lines, recovery-required/recovery-complete counts, sources, and raw error drilldown. Add a 24-hour timechart of `error_events` by host and a host/device recurrence panel. Display collection freshness and storage telemetry separately; do not label a recovery-complete count as a repair-success measure.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. CIM has no documented dataset for ext4 kernel error functions, source lines, or journal-recovery messages. Keep this raw-event search and do not claim a `tstats` equivalent unless the deployment owns and validates a separate normalization.

knownFalsePositives:
A parsed `EXT4-fs error` line is a real kernel-reported filesystem error. The cases below are expected tests, duplicate notifications, or already-contained incidents rather than fabricated errors.

1. **ext4 fault-injection or e2fsprogs qualification lab** — A storage engineer may intentionally corrupt a disposable image or exercise kernel error paths. Confirm the exact lab host, device, kernel build, test owner, procedure, and approved UTC window; route the event to test evidence and never suppress the same signature fleet-wide.

2. **Known damaged volume under active containment** — A quarantined host can emit repeated ext4 errors while an incident awaits backup validation or an offline maintenance window. Match the exact host, device, open incident, and containment state; suppress duplicate notification actions only, retain every raw record, and reopen escalation if the function, device, or impact changes.

3. **Universal Forwarder backlog after outage** — A historical ext4 record can arrive after forwarding resumes. Compare event `_time`, `_indextime`, boot context, source file, and incident history. Preserve the late evidence, repair collection latency, and close only a duplicate page; do not exclude future records from that device.

4. **Overlapping local-file and syslog-relay collection** — The same kernel line may be indexed from `/var/log/messages` and `/var/log/kern.log`, or once locally and once through a relay. Compare host, raw text, event time, source, and `_indextime`; remove the overlapping input instead of adding `dedup`, because two genuine errors can have identical function and detail.

5. **Replayed lab image or cloned log fixture** — Restoring a VM snapshot, test-index replay, or copying archived syslog into a monitored path can re-index an old error. Confirm source path, clone/change record, boot identity where available, and event-versus-index time before downgrading.

**Safe suppression:** if local policy requires notification exceptions, apply an owner-reviewed `linux_ext4_error_exceptions.csv` only in the deployed alert wrapper after extraction. Key it on exact `host`, `device`, and optionally `kernel_function`, with UTC `valid_from`, `valid_until`, `ticket`, `owner`, and `reason`; reject wildcards and expired rows and preserve suppressed base results. The catalogue SPL intentionally has no lookup dependency.
mitreAttack: N/A (operational ext4 filesystem-fault monitoring; no adversary behavior is asserted)
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and signal boundary

Assign a Linux filesystem owner, a storage owner, and a Splunk content owner before enabling paging. Deploy a supported Splunk Universal Forwarder to every in-scope Linux host or use the organization's approved central-syslog design. The collecting service account needs read access to the selected text log and outbound access through the normal forwarding route; the search owner needs access to the selected operating-system index and permission to create a scheduled search and alert action. `index=os` is a local catalogue convention, not a Splunk-required index. No premium app, HEC token, custom shell poller, or CIM acceleration is required.

This rule has a deliberately narrow semantic boundary. Current Linux source emits ext4 errors as `EXT4-fs error (device <id>): <function>:<line>: ...` and, for another error helper, `EXT4-fs error (device <id>) in <function>:<line>: ...`. It emits mount-time journal context separately as `EXT4-fs (<id>): INFO: recovery required on readonly filesystem` and `EXT4-fs (<id>): recovery complete`. The error form includes the word `device`; the recovery form does not. The SPL preserves that distinction instead of searching loose words such as `ext4`, `abort`, or `FS-error`.

Linux documents that ext4 records an error state and first/last error metadata in its superblock and can continue, remount read-only, or panic according to configured policy. Therefore one exact error record is actionable even if the host still answers checks. Conversely, `recovery complete` reports completion of journal replay during mount. e2fsprogs documents that replaying committed journal transactions after an unclean shutdown is not the same as a full consistency check, and further checking can still be required. Never interpret the recovery counter as proof of `e2fsck`, repair success, or device health.

## Step 1 — Configure and qualify kernel-log collection

On each supported distribution image, identify the one persistent text file that actually receives kernel messages. Compare recent `journalctl -k -b` output with `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/kern.log`, and `/var/log/syslog`; select only the authoritative file. A journal-only host is outside this file-monitor procedure until the platform owner implements a supported journal input or journal-to-text/syslog path with its own source-type contract. Do not poll `dmesg`: the kernel ring buffer is finite, can be cleared or overwritten, and repeatedly dumping it can re-index old records.

Package the monitor in a managed deployment app or an approved local override; do not edit a shipped app's `default` directory. For a host where `/var/log/messages` is authoritative, the essential stanza is:

```ini
[monitor:///var/log/messages]
disabled = 0
index = os
sourcetype = linux_messages_syslog
```

Replace the path and index only after verifying the local design. Splunk documents `linux_messages_syslog` as the pretrained source type for standard Linux syslog such as `/var/log/messages`. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux can manage broader `/var/log` collection, but its scripted-input inventory has no dedicated ext4-error input; do not enable `hardware.sh` or invent a dmesg poll for this rule. If the add-on or another deployment app already monitors the selected file, modify that one effective stanza instead of creating a duplicate. The optional structured add-on mapping remains `requiresSmeReview=true` because this documentation review did not install or certify an add-on version.

After deployment, inspect the winning configuration with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`. Search `index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog earliest=-24h | stats count min(_time) as first_event max(_time) as last_event values(source) as sources by host` and reconcile returned hosts and paths with the in-scope inventory. On one representative host per distribution, compare at least two harmless kernel records byte-for-byte and timestamp-for-timestamp between the monitored file, `journalctl -k`, and Splunk. Measure `_indextime-_time`; choose the scheduling delay from observed high-percentile latency. A quiet ext4 detector does not prove collection health, so retain a separate source-freshness control.

Expected indexed fields are `_time`, `_raw`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`. `device`, `event_type`, `kernel_function`, `source_line`, and `error_detail` are search-time outputs of this SPL, not fields promised by the Universal Forwarder, add-on, or CIM. A kernel device such as `dm-0` is not a mount point and can be an unstable mapper name; resolve it through approved host/storage inventory during response.

## Step 2 — Create, understand, and schedule the search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_ext4_errors_5m`. The base terms limit scanning to ext4's exact error prefix and two exact recovery phrases. The first `rex` accepts both kernel-defined error separators, extracts the device, function, source line, and remaining detail, and refuses look-alike application text without that complete shape. The second `rex` handles the different recovery prefix. `coalesce` creates one device field only after one of those parsers succeeds; `case` labels errors, recovery-required, and recovery-complete records without treating warnings or generic I/O messages as equivalent.

The conditional integer fields make the aggregation explicit. `bin` places events into five-minute event-time buckets. `stats` emits one row per bucket, host, and device, counts matching indexed error and recovery records, keeps first/last error times, and retains function, source-line, source-path, detail, and raw-error evidence. The final `where error_events>0` is the alert boundary: recovery-only buckets return no row, while a recovery message in an error bucket is context and never cancels the error. Counts represent indexed records, not distinct corruptions or affected files.

Schedule the search every five minutes with cron `*/5 * * * *` over one completed delayed bucket, initially `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`. Put time bounds in the saved-search dispatch settings or append them consistently to the base search; do not use an overlapping rolling range that pages the same event repeatedly. Trigger when result count is greater than zero. The initial threshold is one parsed ext4 error record per host/device in a completed five-minute window. It has units of indexed records, not errors per second or percentage. There is no defensible healthy baseline for a kernel-reported ext4 error; tune routing and action throttling, not the detection threshold, if a contained device repeats.

Recovery can occur in a later bucket or after reboot, so a zero `recovery_complete_events` value means only that no exact completion record was indexed in the same bucket. Use a drilldown over a wider bounded time range for chronology. Do not join on mount point in the scheduled search, because the kernel signature supplies a device identifier and no authoritative mount field. Do not broaden the rule with `JBD2`, `Buffer I/O error`, `blk_update_request`, or generic `I/O error`; those are valuable adjacent signals but need separately sourced parsers and can affect non-ext4 devices.

## Step 3 — Validate parser, threshold, collection, and recovery semantics

Run the exact positive and negative `controlTest` fixtures in an isolated index with fixed time bounds. The positive error and recovery lines must collapse to exactly one `dm-0` row with one error, one completion, function `ext4_find_entry`, and source line `1458`. Inspect `sample_error_detail` and `sample_error` against the fixture. The negative warning, recovery-only, forced-read-only, and application look-alike records must produce no final rows. Also test the alternate kernel form `EXT4-fs error (device vdb1) in ext4_reserve_inode_write:5932: Journal has aborted`; expect one `vdb1` row with the alternate separator parsed.

Test duplicate visibility rather than hiding it: index the same valid error through two source paths in one bucket and confirm `error_events=2` with both paths in `sources`. This proves why collection overlap can inflate counts. Test malformed lines with no numeric source line and confirm they fail closed; preserve any real rejected sample and extend the parser only after checking the relevant kernel source and adding positive and negative controls.

For collection acceptance, use an existing non-production incident record or a synthetic indexed fixture. Do not corrupt a production filesystem merely to test monitoring. If a storage team has an approved disposable-image fault-injection procedure, record the image, host, kernel and e2fsprogs versions, device, exact action, change ticket, upstream kernel record, indexed event, search job ID, and expected result. This editorial review did not run such an exercise and did not execute SPL in a Splunk runtime.

Do not run `e2fsck` on a mounted production filesystem as a validation step. The upstream e2fsck manual states that checking a mounted filesystem is generally unsafe and that even the narrow read-only exception produces invalid results for a mounted filesystem. An authorized repair must follow the storage owner's offline or vendor-approved procedure. If recovery work occurs, retain the actual command, device identity, preconditions, output, exit status, and post-repair verification; never infer those facts from `recovery complete` alone.

## Step 4 — Alert, visualize, preserve evidence, and respond

Route results to Linux/platform and storage operations, keyed by host and device. Include error count, first/last error, kernel function and source line, source path, raw detail, and a drilldown to surrounding kernel events. A short action throttle may consolidate repeated pages for the exact host/device/incident, but it must not hide another device or discard dispatch results. Keep raw event access restricted according to operational-log policy because neighboring records can reveal device topology, paths, process names, and workload details.

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`. Add a collection-freshness panel sourced from forwarder health, not from absence of ext4 errors. Add storage-adjacent drilldowns for validated SMART/NVMe, multipath, cloud-volume, SAN, hypervisor, and application-write telemetry where those feeds actually exist; do not claim that this rule distinguishes hardware from filesystem corruption by itself.

The response runbook should preserve the exact event and surrounding kernel sequence, identify the current boot and kernel release, resolve the device to stable UUID/WWID and all mount targets, identify affected services, and stop nonessential write retries through owner-approved actions. Check the configured ext4 error policy, recent kernel/filesystem/storage changes, path health, backups, and application impact. Engage the storage owner before changing mounts or devices. Do not automatically remount read-write, clear the journal, reboot, detach storage, run `tune2fs`, or invoke `e2fsck` from the alert. UC-1.1.19 separately handles the exact forced-read-only transition; correlate it when present rather than duplicating that signature here.

Retain the saved-search export, effective input, dispatch result, raw records, fixture outputs, source-coverage report, incident link, recovery decision, and reviewer under the organization's operations-evidence policy. The evidence demonstrates configured behavior and observed events only. It does not establish continuous host coverage, data integrity, regulatory compliance, successful repair, or production certification.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and suppress safely

- **The host has an ext4 error but Splunk has no row:** determine whether the record stayed only in journald, whether the wrong text file is monitored, whether it was routed to another index or sourcetype, whether the search role can see the index, and whether the real message matches one of the two documented kernel forms. Check `_indextime` and forwarding queues before declaring a miss.
- **The event is searchable but `device` is null:** inspect punctuation around `(device ...)`, the `in` versus colon separator, line truncation, and numeric source line. Preserve the sample and verify its kernel branch/source before changing the regular expression; never replace the parser with a loose `ext4 AND error` search.
- **Recovery is zero despite a reboot:** the recovery record may be outside the five-minute error bucket, absent because no journal replay was needed, retained only in another boot's journal, or lost from the selected text log. Search the exact host/device phrase over a bounded wider window. Do not manufacture a completion value or infer repair.
- **Counts are doubled:** compare `source`, `_raw`, `_time`, and `_indextime`; inspect local monitors, broad `/var/log` inputs, and central relays. Remove overlap. Do not add `dedup`, because repeated ext4 errors can legitimately share every parsed field.
- **The alert arrives late or repeats:** compare event and index times, clock synchronization, file flush/rotation, forwarder queues, and saved-search dispatch bounds. Move the completed bucket backward based on measured latency while keeping windows non-overlapping.
- **The host field names a relay:** fix sender attribution in the approved syslog ingestion layer. Do not derive `host` from an unverified token in this search.
- **A contained test or incident is noisy:** use the exact, expiring exception process in `knownFalsePositives` only around notification actions. Preserve base results, require owner and ticket, and reject permanent host-wide or device-wildcard suppression.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for a Linux server reporting that part of its disk filing system has found a serious internal problem. That early warning helps the team protect data and plan a careful repair instead of waiting for programs to fail.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Linux ext4/kernel, e2fsprogs, and Splunk primary sources; synthetic tests specified but not executed in Splunk; no runtime or SME sign-off
